title: BUA201 Principles of Business Administration I

questions.question: The behavioural school of management emerged mainly to address:

options.d: The human and social side of work, such as informal groups and worker attitudes, which earlier classical theories largely ignored

questions.explanation: The behavioural (human relations) school grew out of studies such as the Hawthorne experiments, which showed that social relationships, informal groups and attention to workers affect productivity. Option C is closer to the concern of scientific management, which focused on efficient methods of work rather than people's feelings and group behaviour.

questions.question: In Herzberg's two-factor theory, salary is classified as a:
questions.explanation: Herzberg found that salary, working conditions and company policy are hygiene factors: when poor they cause dissatisfaction, but improving them does not by itself motivate. Option D covers things like achievement, recognition and responsibility, and option A comes from Maslow's hierarchy, not Herzberg.

questions.question: Which historical development most directly led to the separation of ownership from control in business?
questions.explanation: The Industrial Revolution created large factories and enterprises that needed huge capital from many shareholders and professional managers to run them, so owners stopped running the business themselves. Options A and D describe small-scale exchange or self-sufficient production where the owner did everything. Option C was an older trade policy aimed at building national wealth, not a change in how firms were owned and managed.

questions.question: Taylor's Scientific Management has been criticised mainly because it:

options.c: Paid too much attention to workers' social needs

questions.explanation: Scientific management broke jobs into small, timed tasks and assumed money was what drove workers, so critics say it treated people as parts of a machine and ignored their feelings and social needs. Option C is the opposite of the real criticism, since social needs were exactly what it neglected. Options A and D are also wrong, because the approach relied on careful study of tools and methods and strongly promoted specialisation.

questions.question: Which conclusion from the Hawthorne studies challenged classical management theory?
questions.explanation: The Hawthorne studies found that social factors, such as attention from supervisors and the norms of informal work groups, affected output more than physical conditions or pay alone. Option A is the classical assumption the studies challenged. Options C and D were not findings of the studies.

questions.question: A manager who uses strict controls in a crisis but participative methods during stable periods is showing:

options.d: Situational application of Theory X and Theory Y

questions.explanation: Theory X favours close control and Theory Y favours participation, and this manager switches between the two depending on the situation. Options A and B each describe only one side of the behaviour. Option C explains leadership by inborn personal qualities, not by changing style to suit conditions.

questions.question: Which organisational practice aligns MOST with Theory Y?
questions.explanation: Theory Y assumes people can enjoy work, seek responsibility and direct themselves, so it fits practices such as job enrichment and empowerment that give staff more challenge and control. Options A, B and D rest on the Theory X belief that workers must be closely watched and pushed.

questions.question: Modern management thinking emphasises flexibility because organisations operate in:
questions.explanation: Today's businesses face fast changes in technology, competition, regulation and customer tastes, so they must be able to adapt quickly. Options A and D describe conditions where rigid plans could work, which is why they do not explain the need for flexibility. Option C is wrong because modern thinking treats organisations as open systems that interact with their environment.

questions.question: A manager who relies on experience, creativity and judgment while also applying management principles is practising management as:

options.d: Both an art and a science

questions.explanation: Management is a science because it has an organised body of principles, and an art because applying them well takes personal skill, creativity and judgment. This manager combines both. Options A and B each capture only half of what the manager is doing, and option C ignores the principles completely.

questions.question: Who is generally regarded as the father of Scientific Management?
questions.explanation: Frederick W. Taylor developed Scientific Management, which used careful study of tasks, standard methods and incentive pay to raise worker efficiency. Option B is known for the principles and functions of administrative management, option C is linked with the Hawthorne studies and the Human Relations School, and option D is known for the theory of bureaucracy.

questions.question: The Human Relations School of management thought grew mainly out of:

options.d: The Hawthorne studies associated with Elton Mayo

questions.explanation: The Hawthorne studies at the Western Electric company, associated with Elton Mayo, showed that social factors and group relations affect productivity, and this gave rise to the Human Relations School. Option A belongs to Scientific Management, option B to Max Weber, and option C to Henri Fayol, all part of the earlier classical approach.

questions.question: The main focus of Scientific Management was to:

options.a: Satisfy the social needs of workers
options.b: View the organisation as an open system
options.c: Adapt leadership style to each situation
options.d: Raise worker efficiency through systematic study of tasks and methods

questions.explanation: Scientific Management sought the one best way to do each job by studying tasks, standardising methods, selecting and training workers scientifically and linking pay to output. Option A was the focus of the later Human Relations School, option B comes from systems theory, and option C comes from contingency thinking.

questions.question: McGregor's Theory X assumes that the average worker:

options.b: Dislikes work and must be closely supervised and controlled
options.c: Is creative and capable of self-direction

questions.explanation: Theory X holds that people naturally avoid work and responsibility, so managers must direct, watch and sometimes threaten them to get results. Options A, C and D are assumptions of Theory Y, the opposite view of human nature.

questions.question: Which of the following is an assumption of McGregor's Theory Y?

options.b: People avoid responsibility and prefer to be directed
options.c: People can exercise self-direction and self-control when committed to objectives
options.d: People must be threatened with punishment to perform

questions.explanation: Theory Y assumes work can be as natural as play, and that people who are committed to goals will direct themselves, accept responsibility and use their creativity. Options A, B and D are Theory X assumptions, which lead to close supervision and control.

questions.question: A firm that wants to apply Theory Y principles to improve performance would MOST likely:

options.a: Introduce stricter clock-in checks and close supervision
options.b: Involve employees in setting their own goals and give them responsibility for results
options.c: Make all decisions at the top and pass down orders
options.d: Rely mainly on penalties for poor performance

questions.explanation: Theory Y sees employees as willing to work and take responsibility, so managers apply it by involving staff in goal-setting, delegating authority and letting them own their results. Options A, C and D reflect Theory X, which assumes people must be watched, directed and pushed.

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of business?

options.a: It is a one-off exchange made for pleasure
options.b: It is carried on regularly with the aim of making a profit, under risk and uncertainty
options.c: It guarantees a profit to the owner
options.d: It involves only the production of goods, not services

questions.explanation: Business involves the regular production or exchange of goods and services for value, with profit as the main motive, and because the future is uncertain the owner always bears some risk. Option A is wrong because business must be continuous and aimed at gain. Option C ignores risk, and option D ignores the fact that banks, transport firms and other service providers are businesses too.

questions.question: Which of the following activities is a business activity?

options.a: A mother cooking dinner for her family
options.b: A student giving a classmate a book as a birthday gift
options.c: A person selling an old personal phone once to buy a new one
options.d: A trader regularly buying rice in bulk and reselling it at a profit

questions.explanation: A business activity involves the regular exchange of goods or services with the aim of making a profit, which is exactly what the rice trader does. Options A and B involve no exchange for gain, and option C is a one-off personal sale rather than a regular trading activity.

questions.question: The main problem of the barter system, which the use of money helped to solve, was the:

options.a: Lack of any goods to exchange
options.b: Need for a double coincidence of wants

questions.explanation: Under barter, a trade only happens when each person wants exactly what the other has, which is the double coincidence of wants; money removes this problem by acting as a generally accepted medium of exchange. Option A is wrong because goods existed, and options C and D belong to much later, modern business.

questions.question: Any organised activity that provides goods or services to customers on a regular basis with the aim of earning a profit is best described as:
questions.explanation: A business is an organised, continuing activity that supplies goods or services to customers in the hope of earning a profit. Options B and C exist mainly to serve a cause or their members rather than to make profit for owners, and option D is an arm of government that delivers public services rather than a profit-seeking venture.

questions.question: In business, profit is best defined as:

options.a: The money owners invest when starting the business
options.b: The amount a business owes its suppliers
options.c: The total amount of money received from selling goods
options.d: The amount by which total revenue exceeds total expenses

questions.explanation: Profit is what is left after all expenses are taken out of revenue, so it is revenue minus expenses. Option C describes revenue or sales, which ignores costs, option A describes capital, and option B describes trade payables, which is a liability.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a factor of production?
questions.explanation: The factors of production are land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship, the inputs a business combines to produce goods and services. Profit is not an input; it is the reward earned by the entrepreneur. Options B, C and A are all genuine factors of production.

questions.question: The reward paid to the factor of production 'labour' is called:
questions.explanation: Labour is human effort, physical or mental, and it is rewarded with wages or salaries. Option B is the reward for land, option A is the reward for capital, and option D is the reward for entrepreneurship.

questions.question: Chidi uses his savings, rents a shop in Yaba, hires two bakers and buys ovens to start a bread business, knowing he could lose his money if customers do not buy. In doing this, Chidi is acting mainly as:

options.a: A shareholder of a public company

questions.explanation: An entrepreneur organises the other factors of production and bears the risk of loss in the hope of profit, which is exactly what Chidi does. Option C is someone who oversees other workers for an employer, option A merely buys shares in an existing company, and option D buys goods for personal use.

questions.question: A stakeholder of a business is best defined as:

options.a: Any individual or group that can affect or is affected by the business's activities
options.b: Only a person who owns shares in the business
options.c: Only a customer who buys from the business regularly
options.d: Only a person who sits on the board of directors

questions.explanation: Stakeholders include anyone with an interest in the business, such as owners, employees, customers, suppliers, lenders, government and the host community. Options B, D and C each name only one narrow group and wrongly treat it as the whole idea; shareholders are just one type of stakeholder.

questions.question: Which of the following is an INTERNAL stakeholder of a business?
questions.explanation: Internal stakeholders are people inside the organisation, such as employees, managers and owners. Options D, C and B are outside the organisation, so they are external stakeholders even though they are strongly affected by it.

questions.question: A firm in Ogun State turns limestone and other inputs into bags of cement for sale. This firm operates mainly in the:
questions.explanation: The secondary sector covers manufacturing and processing, where raw inputs are converted into finished or semi-finished goods, as in cement production. Option B is extraction of natural resources such as quarrying or farming, option D covers services, and option A refers to government ownership rather than a stage of production.

questions.question: Which of the following businesses belongs to the TERTIARY sector of the economy?
questions.explanation: The tertiary sector provides services rather than physical goods, and banking is a service. Options C and D extract natural resources, so they are primary, while option A manufactures goods, so it is secondary.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT generally regarded as a purpose of business in society?

options.a: Contributing to government revenue through taxes
options.b: Making the laws that govern the country
options.d: Providing goods and services that people need

questions.explanation: Businesses serve society by supplying goods and services, employing people and paying taxes, but law-making is the work of the legislature. Options D, C and A are all genuine ways businesses contribute to society.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of business?

options.a: Exchange of goods or services for value
options.b: Guaranteed returns with no risk of loss

questions.explanation: Every business faces risk and uncertainty, because profit is never guaranteed; that is why the entrepreneur is rewarded for bearing risk. Options A, D and C are standard characteristics of business.

questions.question: Aisha sells her own used laptop once to a friend for N150,000 and makes a gain. This single sale is NOT normally regarded as 'business' mainly because it lacks:
questions.explanation: Business involves dealings carried on regularly or continuously, so a one-off sale of a personal item is not treated as business even if it produces a gain. The sale does involve an exchange, a buyer and a seller and an agreed price, so options B, A and C are present and cannot be the missing feature.

questions.question: Which of the following is an 'aid to trade' within commerce?
questions.explanation: Commerce is made up of trade and the aids to trade, such as banking, insurance, transport, warehousing and advertising, which remove obstacles to exchange. Insurance removes the hindrance of risk. Options D, C and B are production activities in industry, not aids to trade.

questions.question: A non-profit organisation differs from a business mainly because it:

options.a: Uses any surplus to pursue its mission instead of distributing it to owners
options.d: Is never allowed to earn more income than it spends

questions.explanation: A non-profit organisation may earn a surplus, but the surplus is reinvested in its social, religious or charitable mission rather than shared among owners. Option D is wrong because a surplus is allowed, option B is wrong because many non-profits employ paid staff, and option C is wrong because every organisation needs management.

questions.question: Management is often described as the art of:

options.a: Owning the capital of a business

questions.explanation: This classic description stresses that managers achieve goals by working with and through other people rather than doing all the work themselves. Option D describes an operative worker, option B is the opposite of management, and option A describes ownership, which is different from managing.

questions.question: Using the fewest possible resources (time, money, labour) to achieve a given output is called:
questions.explanation: Efficiency means doing things right, that is, getting the most output from the least input. Option A means doing the right things, that is, achieving the goals the organisation set. Options C and B are principles of fair treatment and team spirit, not measures of resource use.

questions.question: In management, 'effectiveness' means:

options.a: Treating every employee exactly the same
options.b: Keeping staff in the same job for a long time
options.c: Achieving the goals the organisation set out to achieve (doing the right things)
options.d: Minimising the cost of every activity (doing things right)

questions.explanation: Effectiveness is about goal attainment, that is, doing the right things. Option D describes efficiency, which is about resource use rather than goal achievement. Options A and B describe the principles of equity and stability of tenure.

questions.question: A Lagos factory produces plastic chairs at the lowest cost per unit in its industry, but customers no longer want that design and most chairs remain unsold. The factory is best described as:
questions.explanation: Low cost per unit shows the factory uses its inputs well, so it is efficient, but it is not achieving the goal of selling products customers want, so it is not effective. Option C reverses the two ideas, option B ignores the unsold stock, and option A ignores the low production cost.

questions.question: Which statement best explains why management is regarded as both an art and a science?

options.a: It can be learnt only from experience and has no principles
options.b: It is practised only by artists and scientists
options.c: Its principles give exactly the same result in every situation
options.d: It rests on a body of organised principles, but applying them well requires personal skill and judgement

questions.explanation: Management is a science because it has a systematic body of knowledge and principles, and an art because using those principles successfully depends on creativity, experience and judgement. Option A denies the science side, option C overstates it, since management principles are flexible rather than exact laws, and option B is a misreading of the terms.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT part of the classical approach to management?
questions.explanation: The classical approach includes scientific management, administrative management and bureaucracy, all of which focus on structure, efficiency and formal rules. The human relations movement came later as a reaction to the classical view and focused on social and psychological needs of workers. Options A, C and B are all classical schools.

questions.question: The main purpose of time and motion study in scientific management was to:

options.a: Design the organisation chart of the whole company
options.b: Find the one best way of doing a job and set a standard time for it
options.c: Decide how much tax a firm should pay
options.d: Measure how happy workers feel about their jobs

questions.explanation: Time and motion study broke a job into its movements, timed them and removed wasteful motions so a standard 'one best way' and standard time could be set. Option D reflects the later human relations interest in worker attitudes, while options C and A have nothing to do with job study.

questions.question: Under Taylor's differential piece-rate system, a worker who produces MORE than the set standard output is:

options.a: Paid at a higher rate per unit
options.b: Paid at a lower rate per unit
options.d: Paid a fixed salary regardless of output

questions.explanation: The differential piece-rate system paid a higher rate per piece to workers who met or beat the standard and a lower rate to those who fell short, to reward productivity. Option D removes the link between output and pay, option B reverses the scheme, and option C is not part of it.

questions.question: A bar chart that shows planned and actual progress of tasks against time, used for scheduling work, is known as a:
questions.explanation: The Gantt chart, developed by Henry Gantt during the scientific management era, shows tasks as bars along a time scale so managers can schedule and monitor work. Option C shows reporting relationships, option B shows proportions of a whole, and option A shows the relationship between costs, revenue and output.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of Henri Fayol's five elements (functions) of management?
questions.explanation: Fayol listed planning, organising, commanding, coordinating and controlling as the elements of management. Staffing was added by later writers, so it is not one of Fayol's five. Options D, C and A are all on Fayol's list.

questions.question: Fayol's principle of 'unity of command' states that:

options.a: Employees should be treated with kindness and justice
options.b: Each employee should receive orders from only one superior
options.c: Each group of activities with the same objective should have one plan and one head
options.d: Authority should flow in an unbroken line from top to bottom

questions.explanation: Unity of command means a subordinate should report to and take orders from one boss only, to avoid confusion. Option C is unity of direction, option D is the scalar chain, and option A is equity.

questions.question: Fayol's principle of 'unity of direction' differs from 'unity of command' because unity of direction requires:

options.a: One head and one plan for a group of activities having the same objective
options.b: Workers to stay in the same job permanently
options.c: All decisions to be taken by the owner alone
options.d: Each worker to report to only one supervisor

questions.explanation: Unity of direction is about the organisation of activities: activities that share one objective should be under one plan and one manager. Option D is unity of command, which is about individual reporting lines. Options C and B describe extreme centralisation and stability of tenure.

questions.question: Bola, a sales officer in a Lagos firm, receives an instruction from the sales manager to visit Ikeja and a conflicting instruction from the finance manager to stay in the office. This situation violates Fayol's principle of:
questions.explanation: Bola is receiving orders from two superiors at once, which is what unity of command is meant to prevent. Option D is about specialisation of tasks, option B is about fair pay, and option A is about allowing employees to think out and carry out plans.

questions.question: The line of authority running from the highest to the lowest rank in an organisation, through which communication normally passes, is Fayol's:
questions.explanation: The scalar chain is the chain of superiors from top to bottom, and Fayol allowed a 'gang plank' for direct communication between people at the same level when delay would be harmful. Option B is team spirit, option A is having a right place for every person and thing, and option D concerns how far decision-making is concentrated at the top.

questions.question: Fayol's principle that stresses building harmony and team spirit among staff is called:
questions.explanation: Esprit de corps means 'union is strength': managers should promote team spirit and unity. Option C is fair and kind treatment of employees, option D is obedience and respect for agreements, and option A is keeping staff turnover low so people can master their jobs.

questions.question: 'A place for everything and everything in its place', applied to both people and things, describes Fayol's principle of:
questions.explanation: The principle of order says every person and every item should have a proper, assigned place in the organisation. Option D is the line of authority, option C is freedom to think out and carry out plans, and option A is fair payment for work.

questions.question: A branch manager refuses a staff member's request to divert company vehicles for a private family event because the firm's goals must come first. This reflects Fayol's principle of:

options.c: Subordination of individual interest to the general interest

questions.explanation: This principle says the interests of one person or group should not take priority over the interests of the organisation as a whole. Option B is about specialisation, option D is about one plan and one head for related activities, and option A is about where decision-making authority lies.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of Max Weber's ideal bureaucracy?

options.a: Selection and promotion based on technical qualification
options.d: Promotion based on personal loyalty to the boss

questions.explanation: Weber's bureaucracy relies on hierarchy, written rules, impersonality and appointment and promotion on merit and competence. Promotion based on personal loyalty contradicts the impersonal, merit-based nature of bureaucracy. Options B, C and A are genuine features.

questions.question: In Weber's ideal bureaucracy, the legitimate basis of authority is:

options.a: Rational-legal authority, based on rules and the position held
options.b: Traditional authority, based on custom and inheritance
options.c: Charismatic authority, based on the personal appeal of the leader
options.d: Coercive authority, based on force and fear

questions.explanation: Weber argued that bureaucracy rests on rational-legal authority, where people obey the rules and the office rather than the person. Options C and B are Weber's other two types of authority, which he saw as less suited to large modern organisations, and option D is not one of his three types.

questions.question: The 'Hawthorne effect' refers to the tendency of workers to:

options.a: Change their behaviour or productivity because they know they are being observed and given attention
options.c: Produce less when lighting is improved
options.d: Work harder only when their pay is increased

questions.explanation: The Hawthorne studies at Western Electric found that productivity rose under many changed conditions because workers responded to the attention and interest shown in them. Option D reflects the purely economic view the studies challenged, option B is not what was found, and option C contradicts the finding that output rose even when lighting changed.

questions.question: The human relations approach to management placed its main emphasis on:

options.a: Using mathematical models to make decisions
options.b: Finding the one best way to perform each task
options.c: Social needs of workers and the influence of informal groups on productivity
options.d: Strict rules and an impersonal hierarchy

questions.explanation: The human relations approach, which grew out of the Hawthorne studies, stressed that workers are social beings whose attitudes, group norms and feelings affect output. Option B is scientific management, option A is the quantitative approach, and option D is bureaucracy.

questions.question: In Maslow's hierarchy of needs, which need is at the TOP of the hierarchy?
questions.explanation: Maslow's order from bottom to top is physiological, safety, social (belonging), esteem and self-actualisation, so self-actualisation, the need to reach one's full potential, is at the top. Option B is just below the top, while options A and C are lower-order needs.

questions.question: The approach to management that uses mathematical and statistical tools such as linear programming and operations research to improve decision-making is the:
questions.explanation: The quantitative or management science approach applies mathematics, statistics and models to management problems such as scheduling and inventory. Option B focuses on people and social needs, option C on principles and functions of management, and option D on rules and hierarchy.

questions.question: In the systems approach, 'synergy' means that:

options.a: A system will always run down without new inputs
options.b: The parts of an organisation working together achieve more than they would working separately
options.c: An organisation has no interaction with its environment
options.d: Each department should work independently of the others

questions.explanation: Synergy is the idea that the whole is greater than the sum of its parts when departments cooperate. Option D contradicts the systems emphasis on interdependence, option C describes a closed system, and option A describes entropy.

questions.question: The contingency (situational) approach to management holds that:

options.a: There is one best way to manage in all situations
options.b: Management is purely a matter of mathematics
options.d: The best management practice depends on the particular situation

questions.explanation: The contingency approach says there is no universal best way; the right structure or style depends on factors such as size, technology and environment. Option A is the classical belief the contingency approach rejects, option C overstates human relations, and option B overstates the quantitative approach.

questions.question: Which sequence shows the correct historical order in which these schools of management thought emerged?

options.a: Contingency approach, scientific management, human relations
options.b: Scientific management, contingency approach, human relations
options.c: Scientific management, human relations, contingency approach
options.d: Human relations, scientific management, contingency approach

questions.explanation: Scientific management emerged around the early 1900s, the human relations movement grew from the Hawthorne studies of the 1920s and 1930s, and the contingency approach developed from the 1960s. Options D, A and B each place at least one school out of its historical order.

questions.question: Managers combine four broad kinds of organisational resources: human, financial, physical and information resources. Which of the following is an INFORMATION resource?

options.d: Market research data on customer preferences

questions.explanation: Information resources are usable data such as market research, sales records and forecasts. Option B is a physical resource, option A is a financial resource, and option C is a human resource.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the resources managers combine to achieve organisational goals?
questions.explanation: Human, financial, physical and information resources are the inputs managers work with. Customer satisfaction is an outcome the business hopes to achieve by using those inputs well, not an input itself. Options B, A and D are genuine resource categories.

questions.question: Chester Barnard's 'acceptance theory of authority' states that a manager's authority depends mainly on:

options.a: Whether subordinates accept the manager's orders
options.b: The manager's share ownership in the firm
options.c: The number of years the manager has spent in the firm
options.d: The size of the manager's salary

questions.explanation: Barnard argued that authority is real only if subordinates accept it, so orders must be understood, consistent with goals and within people's ability. Options D, C and B are personal attributes that do not by themselves make subordinates obey.

questions.question: Management by objectives (MBO), associated with Peter Drucker, is best described as:

options.a: A system in which top management sets all targets without consulting staff
options.b: A method of paying workers per unit produced
options.c: A system in which managers and subordinates jointly set specific goals and later review performance against them
options.d: A mathematical technique for allocating scarce resources

questions.explanation: MBO involves joint goal-setting between superior and subordinate, periodic review of progress and appraisal against the agreed objectives. Option A lacks the participative element that defines MBO, option B is piece-rate pay, and option D describes linear programming.

questions.question: A manager at a Kano textile mill splits the production process into spinning, weaving and dyeing, with workers specialising in one stage each. This applies Fayol's principle of:
questions.explanation: Division of work means specialisation, so that each worker becomes more skilled and productive at a narrower task. Option D concerns having one boss, option C the line of authority, and option B fair treatment of staff.

questions.question: An organisation is best defined as:

options.b: A group of people working together in a structured way to achieve common goals
options.c: Any building where goods are stored
options.d: A collection of individuals with no shared purpose

questions.explanation: An organisation is a deliberate arrangement of people with a common purpose, a structure and a division of tasks. Option C describes a warehouse, option D lacks the shared goal that defines an organisation, and option A is a legal permit.

questions.question: A Lagos supermarket allows its cashiers to suggest and test new ways of reducing queues at the till. This applies Fayol's principle of:
questions.explanation: Initiative means encouraging employees to think out and carry out plans, which raises morale and improvement. Option C concentrates decision-making at the top, option D is obedience and respect for rules, and option B is having a right place for people and things.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: A manager who builds and maintains a network of contacts with external regulators and with managers in other organisations, in order to gain information and goodwill for the unit, is performing which Mintzberg role?
questions.explanation: In Mintzberg's framework, the liaison role is an interpersonal role in which the manager develops and maintains contacts outside his or her own unit. Option D is about passing information to people inside the organisation, while options C and B are decisional roles about starting change and deciding who gets what resources.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: Conceptual skills are most critical when a manager is:
questions.explanation: Conceptual skill is the ability to see the organisation as a whole and think through complex, abstract situations, which is exactly what strategy formulation demands, mostly at top management level. Options B and A lean more on technical skills, and option D relies heavily on human (interpersonal) skills.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: Which of the following is one of Mintzberg's decisional roles?
questions.explanation: Mintzberg's decisional roles are entrepreneur, disturbance handler, resource allocator and negotiator. Options D and B are informational roles, while option A is an interpersonal role.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: The organising function of management involves:
questions.explanation: Organising means arranging work, grouping tasks into jobs and departments, and deciding who reports to whom. Option B belongs to planning, option A to leading, and option D to controlling.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: A mission statement defines an organisation's:
questions.explanation: A mission statement explains why the organisation exists, what it does and whom it serves, guiding all later planning. Options A, D and B are more detailed, short-range plans that flow from the mission.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: A company with a decentralised structure promotes:

options.d: Concentration of authority at the top

questions.explanation: Decentralisation pushes decision-making authority down to lower-level managers who are closer to the problems, so decisions are made more quickly. Option D describes centralisation, and option B is a typical drawback of highly centralised structures.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: Strategic control differs from operational control because it focuses on:
questions.explanation: Strategic control checks whether the organisation's overall strategy is still working and on course over the long term. Options D and A are the concerns of operational control, which deals with day-to-day activities.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: A highly centralised structure limits:
questions.explanation: In a centralised structure most decisions are made at the top, so lower-level staff have little room to take decisions on their own, which limits empowerment. Option A is the opposite, because centralisation concentrates authority in top management. Options C and D can still be carried out, often more tightly, under centralisation.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: Corporate-level strategy differs from business-level strategy because it focuses on:

options.c: Portfolio decisions about which businesses or industries the firm should be in

questions.explanation: Corporate-level strategy is set by top management for the whole organisation and answers the question of which businesses or industries to compete in, including expansion, acquisition and exit. Business-level strategy then decides how each unit competes in its own market. Options A, B and D are operational or functional matters handled lower down.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: A manager who uses systems theory would MOST likely:
questions.explanation: Systems theory sees an organisation as a set of interrelated parts that interact with each other and with the outside environment, so a change in one part affects the others. Options A and C describe a closed-system view that systems theory rejects. Option D reflects the classical one-best-way thinking, not systems thinking.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: Which management function ensures that deviations from plans are corrected?
questions.explanation: Controlling involves setting standards, measuring actual performance, comparing it with the plan and taking corrective action when there are deviations. Option B sets the goals in the first place, option C arranges resources and tasks, and option D guides and motivates people; none of these is the checking-and-correcting function.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: Planning and controlling are closely related because:

options.a: Control provides feedback for future plans
options.b: Both are performed at exactly the same time
options.c: Planning replaces the need for control

questions.explanation: Planning sets the targets that control measures against, and the results of control show where plans worked or failed, which feeds into the next round of planning. Option C is wrong because even good plans need checking, and option D reverses the order, since there is nothing to control until a plan exists. Option B misses the point that one feeds the other.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: The management function that involves setting goals and deciding in advance what to do, how and when to do it, is:
questions.explanation: Planning means defining goals and choosing the courses of action to reach them, so it decides in advance what is to be done. Option D arranges people and resources to carry out the plan, option C motivates and directs people, and option B checks performance against the plan.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: Which management function is usually described as the foundation of the others because it comes first and gives them direction?
questions.explanation: Planning is called the primary function because organising, leading and controlling all depend on the goals and plans it sets; there is nothing to organise or control without a plan. Options D, B and C are important but follow from the plan.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: The MD of a Lagos logistics firm sets a target to open three new depots by December 2026 and decides which cities, budgets and timelines to use. She is performing the function of:
questions.explanation: Setting a target and deciding locations, budgets and timelines in advance is planning. Option B would come next when she assigns staff and resources to each depot, option A when she motivates and directs the teams, and option C when she checks progress against the target.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: After a new strategy is approved, a manager creates departments, assigns tasks to job holders, sets reporting lines and allocates equipment to each unit. This is the management function of:
questions.explanation: Organising means arranging tasks, people and other resources into a structure so the plan can be carried out. Option D set the strategy already, option A involves motivating and influencing people, and option B involves measuring and correcting performance.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: The management function concerned with motivating, communicating with and influencing employees to work towards organisational goals is:
questions.explanation: Leading (also called directing) is about guiding and inspiring people, communicating and resolving conflicts so that they work willingly towards goals. Option A sets the goals, option D designs the structure, and option B monitors results.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: A supervisor at an Abuja call centre holds a morning meeting to encourage her team, explains the day's targets and settles a quarrel between two agents. She is mainly performing the function of:
questions.explanation: Encouraging staff, communicating targets and handling conflict are leading activities. Option C would involve setting the targets in the first place, option B would involve arranging shifts and duties, and option A would involve checking actual performance against the targets.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: Which sequence correctly shows the basic steps in the control process?

options.a: Take corrective action, set standards, compare with standards, measure actual performance
options.b: Compare with standards, measure actual performance, set standards, take corrective action
options.c: Measure actual performance, set standards, take corrective action, compare with standards
options.d: Set standards, measure actual performance, compare performance with standards, take corrective action

questions.explanation: Control starts with standards, because performance cannot be judged without a yardstick; actual results are then measured, compared with the standard, and deviations are corrected. Options C, A and B each place a step before the information it needs is available.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: At the end of each month, the sales manager of an Ibadan distributor compares actual sales of N8,200,000 with the budgeted N10,000,000 and investigates the shortfall. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Comparing actual results with the budget and investigating the gap is controlling, which keeps performance on track. Option D produced the N10,000,000 budget in the first place, option A arranges people and resources, and option C motivates and directs staff.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four functions in the planning-organising-leading-controlling (POLC) framework of management?
questions.explanation: The POLC framework names planning, organising, leading and controlling as the four basic management functions. Bargaining is a negotiation activity, not one of the four functions. Options B, C and D are all part of POLC.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: Which statement best describes the relationship among the management functions?

options.a: They are completely separate and are performed only once each
options.b: Each function is performed by a different level of management only
options.c: Controlling must be finished before any planning can begin
options.d: They are interrelated and continuous, with controlling feeding information back into planning

questions.explanation: The functions overlap and repeat: results from controlling show where plans must be revised, so the process is a continuous cycle. Option A ignores the cyclical nature, option B is wrong because managers at every level perform all four, and option C reverses the usual order.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: The 'universality of management' means that:

options.a: Management principles are laws that never change
options.b: Every manager in the world uses exactly the same style
options.c: Management principles and functions apply to all kinds of organisations and at all levels
options.d: Management is needed only in large profit-making companies

questions.explanation: Universality means planning, organising, leading and controlling are needed in businesses, governments, schools, hospitals, clubs and religious bodies, and at every level. Option D wrongly restricts management to big firms, option B confuses universal functions with identical styles, and option A confuses principles with fixed laws.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: The leader of a church youth fellowship in Surulere sets goals for the year, forms committees, motivates members and reviews each event. This best illustrates:
questions.explanation: The fellowship is not a business, yet its leader performs planning, organising, leading and controlling, which shows that management applies to every kind of organisation. Option B is a line of authority, option C is Weber's model of rules and hierarchy, and option D involves bearing business risk for profit.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: Viewing management from the PROCESS perspective means seeing it as:

options.a: A collection of unrelated tasks with no order
options.b: The legal ownership structure of a company
options.c: A single decision taken once a year
options.d: A continuous series of interrelated functions such as planning, organising, leading and controlling

questions.explanation: The process view treats management as an ongoing set of linked activities that managers perform repeatedly to achieve goals. Option A ignores the link among the functions, option C reduces management to one act, and option B describes forms of ownership.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: From the SYSTEMS perspective, an organisation is viewed as:

options.a: A set of interrelated parts that takes inputs from the environment, transforms them and returns outputs
options.b: A closed unit that does not depend on its environment
options.c: A list of rules that employees must obey
options.d: A group of departments that each work alone

questions.explanation: The systems view sees the organisation as an open system of interdependent subsystems that interacts with its environment through inputs, transformation and outputs, with feedback. Option B describes a closed system, option D ignores interdependence, and option C describes bureaucracy.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: In the systems view of a bakery, which of the following is an INPUT?

options.a: Loaves of bread sold to customers
options.d: Flour, sugar and the bakers' labour

questions.explanation: Inputs are the resources the system takes in, such as raw ingredients, labour, money and information. Option A is the output, option C is the transformation process, and option B is feedback that tells the bakery how its output is received.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: In the systems view of an organisation, 'feedback' refers to:

options.a: Information about outputs that is used to adjust inputs or the transformation process
options.b: The raw inputs bought from suppliers
options.c: The building in which production takes place
options.d: The finished goods delivered to customers

questions.explanation: Feedback is information on how the outputs perform, for example sales figures or customer complaints, which management uses to make corrections. Option B describes inputs, option D describes outputs, and option C is a physical resource.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: An organisation that constantly interacts with and depends on its external environment for resources and customers is described in systems theory as:
questions.explanation: An open system exchanges inputs and outputs with its environment, which is true of every real business. Option D is self-contained and does not interact with its environment, option A is a part of a larger system such as a department, and option B is the tendency of a system to run down.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: A breakdown in the production department of a Lagos beverage company causes the marketing department to miss delivery promises to distributors. This mainly illustrates the systems idea that:

options.a: An organisation is a closed system
options.c: Subsystems of an organisation are interdependent
options.d: Only top managers need to understand the system

questions.explanation: Because the departments are linked subsystems, a problem in one quickly affects the others, which is the core idea of interdependence in systems thinking. Option A contradicts the systems view, option B would make the problem worse, and option D ignores that all managers must coordinate with other units.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: A manager who is responsible for a single specialised area of the business, such as finance, marketing or human resources, is called a:
questions.explanation: A functional manager heads one specialised department, such as finance or marketing. Option C oversees a complex unit that includes several functions, option A coordinates a temporary project team, and option B leads the board rather than a department.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: The head of a regional division of a Nigerian food company is responsible for that division's production, marketing, finance and personnel. She is best described as a:
questions.explanation: A general manager is responsible for a whole unit that contains several functional areas. Option B would head only one function, option C supervises operative workers directly, and option D advises line managers in a specialised field.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: Which of the following shows how management applies across functional areas of a business?

options.a: Marketing managers need no control systems
options.b: Only the finance manager plans; others only carry out orders
options.c: Management functions apply only to the production department
options.d: The production, marketing, finance and HR managers each plan, organise, lead and control within their own areas

questions.explanation: Every functional manager performs all four management functions in their own area; for example, a marketing manager plans campaigns, organises the sales team, leads staff and controls sales results. Options B, C and A wrongly limit management to one function or department.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: Managers responsible for making organisation-wide decisions and setting long-term strategy and policies are:
questions.explanation: Top managers such as the managing director or chief executive set overall direction, strategy and policy for the whole organisation. Option A translates those plans for their units, option B supervises day-to-day work of operatives, and option D are non-managerial staff.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: The main role of MIDDLE managers is to:

options.a: Represent shareholders at the annual general meeting
options.b: Set the overall mission and long-term strategy of the organisation
options.c: Personally perform the routine production work
options.d: Translate top management's goals into specific plans for their units and coordinate first-line managers

questions.explanation: Middle managers stand between top and first-line management, turning broad strategy into departmental plans and coordinating the managers below them. Option B is top management's role, option C is done by operative employees, and option A is not a managerial level role.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: A foreman in a Kaduna factory assigns daily tasks to machine operators, checks their work and reports problems to the production manager. He is a:
questions.explanation: First-line (supervisory) managers direct the daily work of operative employees, as the foreman does. Option A sets strategy for the whole firm, option C manages other managers such as the production manager, and option B serves on the board without running daily operations.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: Which of the following job titles is usually a MIDDLE-level management position?
questions.explanation: A regional sales manager typically reports to top management and supervises area or branch supervisors, which is the middle level. Option C is top management, option B is first-line management, and option D is a non-managerial operative job.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: Compared with first-line managers, top managers generally focus on decisions that:

options.b: Have a longer time horizon and affect the whole organisation
options.c: Concern a single machine or task
options.d: Cover only the next few hours of work

questions.explanation: Top managers deal with strategic decisions covering several years and the whole organisation, while first-line managers handle short-term operational issues. Options D and C describe first-line concerns, and option A describes the skill most needed at the first-line level.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: Henry Mintzberg grouped his ten managerial roles into three categories. These are:
questions.explanation: Mintzberg's ten roles fall into interpersonal, informational and decisional groups. Option D lists Katz's three managerial skills, option B lists management functions, and option A lists types of plans or decisions.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: How many managerial roles did Henry Mintzberg identify?
questions.explanation: Mintzberg identified ten roles, organised into three groups: interpersonal, informational and decisional. Option B is the number of groups, option A is the number of Fayol's elements of management, and option D is the number of Fayol's principles.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: Which of the following roles belongs to Mintzberg's INFORMATIONAL category?
questions.explanation: The informational roles are monitor, disseminator and spokesperson. Option C is an interpersonal role, while options D and A are decisional roles.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of Mintzberg's INTERPERSONAL roles?
questions.explanation: The interpersonal roles are figurehead, leader and liaison. Spokesperson is an informational role, because it involves passing information to outsiders. Options C, A and D are all interpersonal roles.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of Mintzberg's DECISIONAL roles?
questions.explanation: The decisional roles are entrepreneur, disturbance handler, resource allocator and negotiator. Monitor is an informational role, because it involves seeking and receiving information. Options C, A and D are decisional roles.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: The MD of a Nigerian bank cuts the ribbon at a new branch opening and signs certificates for long-serving staff. In Mintzberg's terms, he is performing the role of:
questions.explanation: The figurehead role covers ceremonial and symbolic duties performed because of the manager's position, such as opening branches and signing documents. Option B involves motivating and directing staff, option A involves giving official information to outsiders, and option C involves starting improvement projects.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: A plant manager regularly reads trade journals, reviews daily production reports and listens to suppliers to keep track of what is happening in and around the business. In Mintzberg's terms, this is the role of:
questions.explanation: The monitor role involves seeking and receiving information from inside and outside the organisation. Option A passes information on to subordinates, option D maintains a network of outside contacts, and option C decides how resources are shared.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: After a meeting with top management, a branch manager calls her staff together and passes on the new policy on customer service. In Mintzberg's terms, she is acting as a:
questions.explanation: The disseminator role transmits information received from outside or from above to members of the manager's own unit. Option B transmits information to people outside the organisation, option A gathers information, and option C performs ceremonial duties.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: The head of corporate affairs of a telecom company appears on television to explain to the public why the company's network was down for six hours. In Mintzberg's terms, this is the role of:
questions.explanation: The spokesperson role transmits information about the organisation to outsiders such as the media, regulators and the public. Option C shares information inside the unit, option A motivates staff, and option D bargains with other parties over resources or terms.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: A manager at a Lagos fintech starts a new project to let customers open accounts through a USSD code, looking for ways to improve the business. In Mintzberg's terms, she is acting as an:
questions.explanation: The entrepreneur role involves searching for opportunities and initiating improvement projects or changes. Option D reacts to unexpected crises, option B gathers information, and option C maintains outside networks.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: When fire breaks out in a warehouse and workers threaten to walk off the job, the factory manager immediately takes charge of the crisis. In Mintzberg's terms, this is the role of:
questions.explanation: The disturbance handler role deals with unexpected crises and conflicts that demand immediate corrective action. Option C starts planned improvements, option B decides who gets which resources, and option A performs ceremonial duties.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: A divisional head decides how the year's N50,000,000 budget will be shared among the sales, production and training units. In Mintzberg's terms, this is the role of:
questions.explanation: The resource allocator role decides who gets the organisation's money, people, time and equipment. Option D involves bargaining with others, option C passes information to subordinates, and option A involves motivating and guiding staff.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: The HR director of a manufacturing firm meets union officials to agree a new wage settlement for workers. In Mintzberg's terms, she is acting as a:
questions.explanation: The negotiator role represents the organisation in major bargaining, such as wage agreements with unions or contracts with suppliers. Option D only transmits information to outsiders, option B maintains contacts for information and favours, and option C handles sudden crises rather than planned bargaining.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: A departmental manager hires a new officer, trains her and praises staff who meet their targets. In Mintzberg's terms, this is the role of:
questions.explanation: The leader role covers hiring, training, motivating and directing subordinates. Option B is ceremonial, option D is about gathering information, and option A is about distributing resources.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: Robert Katz identified three basic skills that managers need. These are:
questions.explanation: Katz described technical, human (interpersonal) and conceptual skills as the basic managerial skills. Option A names Mintzberg's role groups, option B names management functions, and option D is not Katz's classification.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: The ability to use the tools, techniques and specialised knowledge of a particular field, such as accounting or engineering, is called:
questions.explanation: Technical skill is know-how in a specific discipline or method. Option C is the ability to see the organisation as a whole and think abstractly, option B is the ability to work well with people, and option D is not one of Katz's three skills.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: The ability to work well with others, communicate, motivate and build cooperation within a team is called:
questions.explanation: Human (interpersonal) skill is the ability to understand, work with and motivate people, individually and in groups. Option A relates to specialised know-how, option B to seeing the big picture, and option C is not one of Katz's three basic skills.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: The ability to see the organisation as a whole, understand how its parts relate to each other and to the environment, and think in abstract terms is called:
questions.explanation: Conceptual skill is the 'big picture' ability to analyse complex situations and see how the parts fit together. Option A is specialised know-how, option B is the ability to work with people, and option D is not one of Katz's skills.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: Which managerial skill is generally considered MOST important for first-line managers?
questions.explanation: First-line managers supervise operative work directly, so they need strong technical knowledge of how the work is done. Option A becomes more important as one rises to top management, and options C and D are not among Katz's three basic skills.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: Which of Katz's managerial skills is generally considered roughly EQUALLY important at all levels of management?
questions.explanation: Managers at every level work with and through people, so human skill is about equally important at the top, middle and first-line levels. Option D matters most at lower levels and option C matters most at the top, while option A is a technical speciality rather than one of Katz's skill groups.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: The CEO of a Nigerian conglomerate studies how a new import ban, rising interest rates and a rival's expansion will together affect each of the group's businesses. She is mainly using:
questions.explanation: Seeing how many external forces and internal units fit together and affect the whole organisation requires conceptual skill. Option D is specialised know-how in a particular field, option A concerns dealing with people, and option C is not one of Katz's skills.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: A new production supervisor calmly settles a quarrel between two operators and persuades them to work together again. He is mainly using:
questions.explanation: Resolving conflict and getting people to cooperate is human skill. Option C would be shown by repairing a machine or explaining a procedure, option D by analysing how the whole organisation is affected, and option A is not one of Katz's three skills.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: As a manager moves from first-line to top management, the relative importance of technical and conceptual skills generally changes as follows:

options.a: Technical skill becomes more important and conceptual skill becomes less important
options.b: Both stay exactly the same at every level
options.d: Technical skill becomes less important and conceptual skill becomes more important

questions.explanation: Higher-level managers spend less time on specialised operational tasks and more time on strategy, so the need for conceptual skill rises while the need for technical skill falls. Option A reverses the pattern, option C ignores the rising need for conceptual skill, and option B ignores the shift altogether.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: When managers are described as 'organisational stabilisers', it means that they:

options.c: Maintain order, continuity and predictable operations so the organisation keeps running smoothly
options.d: Resist every form of change in the organisation

questions.explanation: As stabilisers, managers keep routines, rules and coordination in place so that work continues reliably even when the environment changes. Option D is wrong because stability does not mean blocking all change, and options A and B describe an absence of management.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: During a period of fuel scarcity, the operations manager of a transport company reorganises schedules, secures alternative suppliers and keeps buses running so services continue normally. This best shows the manager acting as:
questions.explanation: The manager is protecting continuity and keeping operations steady despite disruption, which is the stabilising role of managers. Option B refers to ceremonial duties, option A is a partner who takes no part in management, and option D is an outsider brought in for advice.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: A person who plans, organises, leads and controls the work of others so that organisational goals are achieved is called a:
questions.explanation: A manager coordinates and oversees the work of other people to accomplish organisational goals. Option D performs tasks directly without overseeing others, option A owns shares and may not manage at all, and option C buys the organisation's goods or services.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: Which of the following correctly matches a management function with an example activity?

options.a: Controlling: checking whether production costs are within budget
options.b: Planning: settling a quarrel between workers
options.d: Organising: praising a worker for good performance

questions.explanation: Checking costs against the budget compares actual performance with a standard, which is controlling. Option B is a leading activity, option D is also leading because it motivates, and option C is planning.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: Which of the following best shows that controlling and planning are linked in the management process?

options.a: Controlling replaces the need for organising
options.b: Controlling is done only by the board of directors
options.c: Deviations found during controlling lead managers to revise their plans
options.d: Plans are never changed once made

questions.explanation: Controlling compares results with plans; when results fall short, managers use the information to correct actions or revise the plans, closing the management cycle. Option B wrongly limits control to the board, option D ignores feedback, and option A confuses two distinct functions.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: A production manager at a Lagos bottling plant notices that bottles are leaving the line under-filled and immediately adjusts the filling machine. Which step of the control process is she performing?
questions.explanation: Adjusting the machine fixes the deviation between actual and standard fill levels, which is the corrective-action step of control. Option B comes at the start of control before measurement, option C is planning, and option D is organising.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: In Mintzberg's framework, the role in which a manager builds and maintains a network of contacts outside his or her own unit to obtain information and favours is the:
questions.explanation: The liaison role is about networking with people outside the manager's own unit, both inside and outside the organisation. Option D deals with the manager's own subordinates, option A passes information down to them, and option B decides how resources are shared.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: Which of the following correctly pairs a Mintzberg role with its category?
questions.explanation: Negotiator is a decisional role, alongside entrepreneur, disturbance handler and resource allocator. Option D is wrong because figurehead is interpersonal, option A because monitor is informational, and option C because spokesperson is informational.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: Although managers at all levels perform all four management functions, how does the time spent on them typically differ by level?

options.a: Top managers spend relatively more time planning, while first-line managers spend relatively more time leading and directing day-to-day work
options.b: Every level spends exactly the same share of time on each function
options.c: First-line managers do no controlling at all
options.d: Top managers spend all their time leading, while first-line managers only plan

questions.explanation: All managers plan, organise, lead and control, but top managers concentrate more on planning and organising for the whole organisation, while first-line managers spend more time directing and supervising operatives. Option D reverses the pattern, option C is wrong because supervisors constantly check work, and option B ignores the difference in emphasis.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: In the systems view of a commercial bank, which of the following is part of the TRANSFORMATION process?

options.a: Assessing loan applications and processing customers' transactions
options.b: Customers' deposits and the skills of staff
options.c: Customer complaints received through the call centre
options.d: Satisfied customers and profit for the year

questions.explanation: Transformation is the work that converts inputs into outputs, such as processing transactions and evaluating loans in a bank. Option B lists inputs, option D lists outputs, and option C is feedback from customers.

questions.topic: Universality of Management and Managerial Roles
questions.question: The formal framework of jobs, departments, reporting relationships and lines of authority that results from the organising function is called the:
questions.explanation: Organising produces an organisation structure, often shown on an organisation chart, which sets out who does what and who reports to whom. Option D is the output of planning, option A is a financial plan, and option C is a yardstick used in controlling.

questions.question: In Lewin's three-step model of change, the "refreezing" stage ensures:

options.b: Stabilisation of the change so new behaviours become the norm

questions.explanation: Lewin's model runs unfreeze, change (move), then refreeze; refreezing locks in the new ways of working through policies, rewards and culture so people do not slip back. Option A is the opposite of refreezing, and option C is a problem that unfreezing tries to reduce.

questions.question: Nigeria's banking consolidation of 2004-2005, when the Central Bank of Nigeria under Governor Charles Soludo raised banks' minimum capital base and the number of banks fell from 89 to 25, is best described as:

options.d: Market exit by the banking sector

questions.explanation: Raising the capital requirement more than tenfold forced mergers, acquisitions and closures that reshaped the whole industry within about two years, which is radical change. Options B and C describe small step-by-step adjustments, and option D is wrong because the sector was restructured, not abandoned.

questions.question: In the 2004 Nigerian banking consolidation led by CBN Governor Charles Soludo, the minimum capital base for banks was raised from N2 billion to:
questions.explanation: Banks were required to raise their minimum capital base from N2 billion to N25 billion, a target that pushed many smaller banks to merge. Options A, C and B are not the figure set for that reform.

questions.question: Resistance to change in organisations is often rooted in:
questions.explanation: People often resist change because they do not know how it will affect their jobs, status or routines, and the unknown feels threatening. Options D, C and A would, if anything, make change easier to accept.

questions.question: Corporate restructuring may involve:
questions.explanation: Corporate restructuring means reorganising a company's structure, operations or ownership to improve performance, and downsizing (cutting staff or units) is one of its common forms. Options A and B are economy-wide conditions or government policies, not actions a company takes on itself. Option D is a marketing technique for dividing customers into groups, not a restructuring move.

questions.question: Organisational learning supports:
questions.explanation: Organisational learning is the process by which a firm gains, shares and uses new knowledge, which helps it improve and come up with new ideas, products and methods. Options A and B describe rigidity that learning helps to overcome. Option C is when a firm's strategy falls out of step with its environment, which is what happens when an organisation stops learning.

questions.question: A very common cause of resistance to organisational change is:
questions.explanation: People often resist change because they are unsure how it will affect their jobs, skills or status, and that uncertainty breeds fear. Option C is wrong because clear, frequent communication usually reduces resistance, and option D supports change rather than blocking it. Option B may be a reason for change, not a cause of people resisting it.

questions.question: Which approach is MOST effective in reducing resistance to change?
questions.explanation: When employees take part in planning and carrying out a change, they understand it better and feel ownership of it, which builds commitment. Options A, C and D may force short-term compliance, but they damage trust and often create more resistance later.

questions.question: Compared with an external consultant, an internal change agent is more likely to face resistance because:

options.a: The agent always lacks technical skills
options.b: The agent has no authority at all
options.c: Outside parties interfere with the agent's work
options.d: Colleagues may see the agent as too close to existing relationships and politics to be objective

questions.explanation: An internal change agent knows the organisation well, but colleagues may see him or her as part of existing friendships, rivalries and politics, so the agent's proposals can be viewed as biased. Option A and option B are overstatements, since internal agents are often skilled managers with formal authority. Option C describes outside interference, which is not what makes an insider's position difficult.

questions.question: Which role is LEAST associated with a change agent?
questions.explanation: A change agent's job is to move the organisation from its current state to a better one, so preserving structures exactly as they are runs against that role. Options A, B and C are typical change-agent roles: finding what needs to change, keeping people informed and helping the change take hold.

questions.question: Change management is BEST described as:

options.a: A structured approach to moving individuals and the organisation from the current state to a desired future state
options.b: Keeping the organisation exactly as it is
options.c: Replacing all employees with new ones
options.d: Changing the company's name and logo only

questions.explanation: Change management is the planned process of preparing, supporting and guiding people and the organisation through a transition so that the change is adopted and lasts. Option B is the opposite of change. Options C and D are extreme or superficial actions, not a managed process.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a cause of resistance to change?

options.a: Clear communication and involvement of employees in the change
options.d: Threats to existing status and power

questions.explanation: Clear communication and involvement are ways of reducing resistance, because they help people understand the change and feel part of it.
